title: Surviving Survival Analysis
text:
Preface
How long until something happens? How long until a patient dies, a machine breaks down, a customer cancels their subscription, or a piece of equipment fails. These “time until X” questions seem simple, but they trip up standard statistical methods in ways that are easy to miss and hard to undo. This issue is one of the more common and consequential mistakes in applied statistics, and it has its own dedicated toolkit for a reason.
This workshop will cover Foundations: what makes time to event data different, and why it needs specialised methods. Non parametric estimation: Kaplan Meier curves and log rank tests, including how to interpret and visualise them. Semi parametric modeling: the Cox proportional hazards model, hazard ratios, and checking the proportional hazards assumption. Extensions (time permitting): parametric survival models.
Participants will work through live coded examples and short guided exercises in R, using realistic datasets, and will leave with a working script they can adapt to their own time to event data.

title: Surviving Survival Analysis
text:
About this workshop
This workshop offers a practical, code first introduction to survival analysis using R. We will build up from first principles to applied modeling.
Format: 3 hours, mix of live coding, guided exercises, and Q&A.
Requirements:
- A laptop with a recent R installation and RStudio or similar IDE installed.
- Some familiarity with R and basic regression (for example linear or logistic regression models) is assumed.
- No prior survival analysis experience is necessary.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.2 What is Survival Analysis?
Survival analysis involves analysing time-to-event data. This may be survival of a patient, but it may also be applied to any data where we have measured the time taken to record an event, such as machine failure, customer churn etc.
This combines two things:

An event/non-event indicator and;

The time taken for the event to occur/not occur.

A common task is analysing binary outcome data for events (yes/no, 0/1 etc). There are a range of popular methods for this task. What they all have in common, is that we are definitively classifying each subject into one class or another - so in effect, all subjects have concluded their follow up period. This doesn’t help us understand the probability of these events over time. It also doesn’t help us if subjects drop-off (a real-world issue).
Conversely, we can analyse times as a continuous value, just like any other continuous, positive value. However we can’t just analyse the event times. We also need to measure the times when subjects were lost to follow up. Why? If we don’t we are biasing our estimates by removing subjects who haven’t yet experienced an event. We can’t understand how long things survive by analysing only those who die.
So we need a way of combining a binary event data and continuous time data.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
1.3 Dealing with events
Typically an event is encoded as a binary status indicator variable where the status indicator, normally 0 = alive, 1 = dead. Other choices are TRUE/FALSE (TRUE = death) or 1 = alive, 2 = dead.






Useless Fact



The use of 1/2 for alive/dead instead of the usual 0/1 is a historical footnote. For data contained on punch cards, IBM 360 Fortran treated blank as a zero, which led to a policy within the section of Biostatistics to never use “0” as a data value since one could not distinguish it from a missing value. The policy became a habit, as is often the case; and the 1/2 coding endured long beyond the demise of punch cards and Fortran.


While some subjects will experience an event, for other subjects, their survival times will be unknown. This can occur if a study concludes and some subjects have not yet recorded an event. Alternatively some subjects may drop out and be lost to follow up.
We still need a way to record the time when they didn’t experience the event - which is a weird thing to think about.
For example, A trial follows 200 patients for 5 years to see how long they survive after starting a new cancer drug. When the study ends, some patients are still alive. For those patients, you know they survived at least 5 years, but you don’t know their actual survival time. It could be 5.1 years or 20 years.
This is known as censoring. The most common form is right censoring (as above). There is also left censoring and interval censoring (these are beyond the scope of the workshop).
So, our event indicator is actually event = 1, censored = 0.






Exercise: Classroom Discussion



How should we handle censoring?






a) Pretend censored times are events.





We know the event hasn’t occurred. It might still occur, but the event time will be longer then the censoring time, so it will bias the results.









b) Drop censored observations from the analysis.





Keeping only subjects who experienced the event will understate survival estimates as we don’t incorporate those at risk who haven’t (and don’t) experience the event.









c) Analyse the outcomes as binary events.





This is essentially what logistic regression does. It assumes the negative class explicitly states the event did not occur. This is fine if there is a consistent and definitive follow up period. But in many cases we have varying follow up times. Someone who just enrolled in a clinical trial has had less exposure. This will bias events occurring to those with longer follow up times.









d) Use survival analysis





The methods we will learn allow us to measure and model survival times, while accounting for censoring in our dataset.







1.3.1 Dealing with times
Where does the time variable come from? Often we have staggered start times or deal with cohorts. Survival analysis typically is performed with a consistent follow up time. Below is an example of how we might create this time variable from dates.






Figure 1.1: Converting calendar time in the ovarian cancer study to a survival analysis format. Dashed vertical line is the date of the last follow-up, R=relapse, D=death from ovarian cancer, Do=death from other cause, A=attended last clinic visit (alive), L=loss to follow-up, X=death, □=censored. Source: Clark, T., Bradburn, M., Love, S. et al. Survival Analysis Part I: Basic concepts and first analyses. Br J Cancer 89, 232–238 (2003). https://doi.org/10.1038/sj.bjc.6601118

Expressing this in some units can be done using either Durations or Periods. Durations are consistent mathematically, however Periods may map onto our intuition of the date-time line a little better. title: 2  Non Parametric Modelling
text:
2.1 Kaplan-Meier Estimator
We want to obtain some estimate of the survival of subjects in our data. Defining a survival function will help us describe the probability of survival at a given time \(S(t)\)
A commonly used method to describe the survival or subjects in our data, without making concrete assumptions about the distributions in our data, is the Kaplan-Meier Estimator1.
We can use the observed data to estimate the conditional probability of confirmed survival at each observed survival time. We need to do this for each interval to correctly account for how many subjects remain ‘at risk’ due to an event or censoring. We can multiply these conditional probability estimates together to form our estimated survival function \(\hat{S}(t)\).
Remember, we have a random variable \(T\) representing time. The probability density function of \(T\) is given by \(f(t)\).
\[
P(t \le T < t + dt) \approx f(t)\,dt
\]
As usual, the cumulative density function is given by \(F(t)\).
\[
F(t) = P(T \le t) = \int_0^t f(u)\,du
\]
It is usually more interesting to talk about the probability of survival, rather than the probability of cumulative failure. We can see that:
\[
S(t)= P(T > t)
\]
and so
\[
S(t) = 1 - F(t)
\]

title: 2  Non Parametric Modelling
text:
2.1.1 Example
Let’s take our aml data and sort it ascending by event time (We can ignore the grouping for now).
Splitting the data into intervals, based on each event time we can count how many death events ‘d’ and how many censoring events ‘c’ in each interval between events. Next, at each time increment we need to calculate \(n\) the number at risk. This involves taking the number at risk at the previous event time and subtracting any subjects who died or were censored in the last period. Doing it this way ensures our denominator is correct when calculating survival probabilities.

km1 <- aml |> 
  select(-x) |> 
  arrange(time) |> 
  count(time, status) |> 
  pivot_wider(names_from = status, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |> 
  select(time, d = `1`, c = `0`)

km1

# A tibble: 18 × 3
    time     d     c
   <dbl> <int> <int>
 1     5     2     0
 2     8     2     0
 3     9     1     0
 4    12     1     0
 5    13     1     1
 6    16     0     1
 7    18     1     0
 8    23     2     0
 9    27     1     0
10    28     0     1
11    30     1     0
12    31     1     0
13    33     1     0
14    34     1     0
15    43     1     0
16    45     1     1
17    48     1     0
18   161     0     1








Caution



Remember, when calculating the conditional survival probability, the event and the censoring happen at the event time, so we don’t subtract them from the risk set until the next interval.


We can calculate estimated probability of survival in each interval \(i\) as \(\frac{n_i - d_i}{n_i}\).
The estimated survival function is simply the multiplication of these conditional survival probabilities for each interval.
\[
\hat{S}(t) = \prod_{t_i \leq t}{\frac{n_i - d_i}{n_i}}
\]






Exercise



Calculate the Kaplan-Meier estimator manually in excel for the aml data.
The solution is implemented in R in the next section.

text:
2.2 Calculating Kaplan-Meier Estimator in R

2.2.1 Making a survival object
Turning time-to-event data into a ‘survival’ object with the Surv() function.

head(aml)

  time status          x
1    9      1 Maintained
2   13      1 Maintained
3   13      0 Maintained
4   18      1 Maintained
5   23      1 Maintained
6   28      0 Maintained



Surv(time = aml$time, event = aml$status)

 [1]   9   13   13+  18   23   28+  31   34   45+  48  161+   5    5    8    8 
[16]  12   16+  23   27   30   33   43   45 




2.2.2 Kaplan-Meier Survival function estimate
Normally this Surv() object is wrapped in another function. Here we use the survfit() function to fit a survival curve. For now let’s ignore the x grouping column in the data.

km <- survfit(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = aml) 

This gives us survival summary stats at various time points.

summary(km)

We can specify a time point we care about, for example, 30-day survival.

Call: survfit(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = aml)

 time n.risk n.event survival std.err lower 95% CI upper 95% CI
   30      9      12    0.442    0.11        0.272        0.718








Exercise: If we ignored censoring, what would the survival probability be at time 30?





If we calculate the number of deaths at or before time = 30, divided by the number of subjects, we get the cumulative incidence. Subtracting from 1 gives us a naive estimate for survival. However, note that we have had three subjects drop out before time = 30. This means they are not in the risk set after their drop out time, so we need to remove them from the denominator. This will reduce the survival probability - and ignoring this overstates the survival estimate.

1 - (sum(aml[aml$time <= 30, "status"]) / nrow(aml))

[1] 0.4782609

title: 2  Non Parametric Modelling
text:
2.3 Graphing the Kaplan-Meier Curve
Plot a Kaplan-Meier curve. We get 95% confidence intervals produced also.

plot(km)








There is nothing magic happening here. Let’s do this manually with ggplot2::geom_step()

km_df <- data.frame(
  time   = km$time,
  surv   = km$surv
)

head(km_df)

  time      surv
1    5 0.9130435
2    8 0.8260870
3    9 0.7826087
4   12 0.7391304
5   13 0.6956522
6   16 0.6956522



ggplot(km_df, aes(x = time, y = surv)) +
  geom_step() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  theme_minimal()








More enhanced plots can be made with {ggsurvfit}






Note



The survfit2() function is used instead of survfit(). This is a wrapper of the original function that helps with more advanced downstream calculations.



survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = aml) |>
  ggsurvfit()








The {ggsurvfit} allows us to add useful layers such as confidence intervals, risk tables and quantiles.

survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = aml) |>
  ggsurvfit() +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  add_risktable() +
  add_quantile(y_value = 0.5, color = "gray50") +
  scale_ggsurvfit()

title: 2  Non Parametric Modelling
text:
2.4 Comparing Two Survival Functions
Often we want to compare groups. In our aml data the x column indicates if the standard course of chemotherapy should be extended (‘maintainance’) for additional cycles.
How do the estimated survival functions compare?

aml 

   time status             x
1     9      1    Maintained
2    13      1    Maintained
3    13      0    Maintained
4    18      1    Maintained
5    23      1    Maintained
6    28      0    Maintained
7    31      1    Maintained

9    45      0    Maintained
10   48      1    Maintained
11  161      0    Maintained
12    5      1 Nonmaintained
13    5      1 Nonmaintained
14    8      1 Nonmaintained
15    8      1 Nonmaintained
16   12      1 Nonmaintained
17   16      0 Nonmaintained
18   23      1 Nonmaintained
19   27      1 Nonmaintained
20   30      1 Nonmaintained
21   33      1 Nonmaintained
22   43      1 Nonmaintained
23   45      1 Nonmaintained


We can alter the survfit2() function to draw separate Kaplan-Meier curves for each group.

1survfit2(Surv(time, status) ~ x, data = aml) |>
  ggsurvfit() +
  add_confidence_interval() +
  add_risktable() +
  add_quantile(y_value = 0.5, color = "gray50", linewidth = 0.75) +
  scale_ggsurvfit()   


1

Note the inclusion of the variable after the ~.











The survdiff() function lets us run a logrank test. This is a hypothesis test to test if there is a difference between two or more survival curves. This type of test works similar to a Chi-Square test for independence, and provides a p-value. A p-value below our chosen threshold provides evidence to reject the null hypothesis that the curves are similar.

logrank_test <- survdiff(Surv(time, status) ~ x, data = aml)

logrank_test

Call:
survdiff(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ x, data = aml)

x=Maintained    11        7    10.69      1.27       3.4
x=Nonmaintained 12       11     7.31      1.86       3.4

title: 3  Semi-Parametric Modelling
text:
3.1 Basic theory of survival/hazard curves
In the previous section we explored an effective method for univariate analysis, and even extended this to comparing a few discrete groups e.g. disease categories, sex, age groups. Can we extend this to studying the effects of a number of covariates, similar to how we do regression modelling?
Starting with just survival times, we can define the probability density of survival times as \(f(t)\), where:
\[P(t \le T < t + dt) \approx f(t)\,dt\]
\[f(t) \ge 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \int_0^\infty f(t)\,dt = 1\]
This is the unconditional probability of experiencing the event when viewed from time 0.
It’s often more interesting to understand the cumulative density function:
\[F(t) = P(T \le t) = \int_0^t f(u)\,du\]
This describes the probability of an event happening at some time before time \(t\).
It’s often even more interesting to talk about the probability of survival, rather than the probability of cumulative failure.
\[S(t) = P(T > t) = 1 - F(t) = \int_t^\infty f(u)\,du\]
It’s often even, even more interesting to think about the hazard function. If we ask, what is the probability of a subject dying at 5 years, it’s obvious that the subject was alive up until year 4. So it’s natural to ask about the instantaneous hazard of dying at year 5, conditional of being alive until year 5. This is different to asking about the unconditional probability density of a subject dying at exactly 5 years. The hazard function incorporates ageing and knowledge accumulated throughout the study and provides information more relevant to making decisions through time.
We can define the hazard function as
\[
h(t) = \frac{f(t)}{S(t)}
\]
This is essentially the unconditional probability of seeing an event at time t, scaled by the survival of subjects up until time \(t\).
We can define the cumulative hazard function as
\[H(t) = \int_0^t h(u)\,du\]
This is a little like the accumulated hazard, or the cumulative force of mortality.
Differentiating \(S(t) = 1 - F(t)\) gives
\[S'(t) = -f(t)\]
So
\[f(t) = -S'(t)\]
Substituting into the hazard function:
\[h(t) = \frac{-S'(t)}{S(t)} = -\frac{d}{dt}\log S(t)\]
(This result is due to the chain rule)
Substituting this expression back into our cumulative hazard function we get:
\[\int_0^t h(u)\,du = -\int_0^t \frac{d}{du}\log S(u)\,du = -\big[\log S(u)\big]_0^t = -\log S(t) + \log S(0)\] As \(S(0) = 1\), we have \(\log S(0) = 0\), so
\[H(t) = -\log S(t)\]
Rearranging we get back to the survival function:
\[\boxed{S(t) = e^{-H(t)}} \tag{3.1}\]
It should now be clear there is a close relationship between the density function, hazard function and suvival function. If one is able to specify the hazard function, then the cumulative hazard, and hence, the survival function are also specified.

title: 3  Semi-Parametric Modelling
text:
3.2 Cox Proportional Hazards Model
We are often in a setting where we may wish to see if survival is more favorable under a “new” treatment when compared with the “standard.” We need a model to compare the relative survival experience of the two treatment groups, and give us the ability to adjust for other patient characteristics.
Fully parametric models (models that explicitly describe the statistical distribution of the hazard function) can certainly be used to accomplish this goal. However, these added assumptions are often not required and require more justification.
Survival time models that have a fully parametric regression structure but leave their dependence on time unspecified are called semi-parametric regression models. The most common is the Cox proportional hazards model.
If we start with a constant hazard function with respect to time:
\[
h(t) = 0.3
\] A common parameterisation is to ensure that this value is positive by letting the hazard rate at baseline be \(\beta_0\) and taking the exponent so we have
\[
h(t) = e^{\beta_0}
\] It would be great to add other covariates to this function
\[
h(t, x) = e^{\beta_0 + \beta_x}
\]
If we take \(e^{\beta_0}\) as our baseline hazard rate
\[
h(t, x) = e^{\beta_0}e^{\beta_1x} \\
= h_0(t)e^{\beta x}
\] The hazard function originally expressed is actually the product of two functions, the baseline hazard \(h_0(t)\), which characterizes how the hazard function changes as a function of time. The other function, characterizes how the hazard function changes as a function of the covariates.
We can compute the hazard ratio (HR) as
\[
HR(t, x_1, x_0) = \frac{h(t, x_1)}{h(t, x_0) }
\]
\[
HR(t, x_1, x_0) = \frac{h(t_0)e^{\beta x_1}}{h(t_0)e^{\beta x_0}}
\] Notice how the baseline hazard function \(h(t_0)\) cancels out.
\[
HR(t, x_1, x_0) = \frac{e^{\beta x_1}}{e^{\beta x_0}} \\
= e^{\beta(x_1 - x_0)}
\]
In the above example, is \(x\) is a dichotomous variable e.g. \(x_1 = 1\) for female and \(x_0 = 0\) for male we have
\[
HR(t, x_1, x_0) = e^\beta
\]
We can see three important results:

The hazard ratios are obtained directly from the regression coefficients (which we will learn to fit soon).

There is no dependence on time, as the baseline hazard rate cancelled out.

This is called a proportional hazards model as there is a multiplicative relationship with covariate values and the baseline hazard.

The implication here, are the assumptions around the proportional effect being constant over time.






Note



Note: We haven’t discussed covariates that may change over time, this is a common extension that we will cover later.

title: 3  Semi-Parametric Modelling
section: 3.3 Fitting a Cox Proportional Hazards Model
text:
3.3 Fitting a Cox Proportional Hazards Model
We fit a Cox PH model using coxph() from the {survival} package. The response is a Surv object encoding the event time and censoring indicator, exactly as used in the Kaplan-Meier estimator. We’ll use the lung dataset, which contains survival data from an NCCTG lung cancer trial with several patient-level covariates.
The model we are fitting is
\[
h(t) = h_0(t) \exp{(\beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + ...)}
\] The coxph() function estimates the partial likelihood — it finds \(\hat{\beta}\) without needing to specify or estimate the baseline hazard \(h_0(t)\). That is the key advantage of the Cox model: it is semiparametric in that the baseline hazard is left completely unspecified.
We will be using the lung dataset from the {survival} package. This dataset measures survival in patients with advanced lung cancer from the North Central Cancer Treatment Group. For more information see Section 1.4.

cox_fit <- coxph(
  Surv(time, status) ~ sex + age,
  data = lung
)

summary(cox_fit)

Call:
coxph(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ sex + age, data = lung)

  n= 228, number of events= 165 

         coef exp(coef)  se(coef)      z Pr(>|z|)   
sex -0.513219  0.598566  0.167458 -3.065  0.00218 **
age  0.017045  1.017191  0.009223  1.848  0.06459 . 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

    exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
sex    0.5986     1.6707    0.4311    0.8311
age    1.0172     0.9831    0.9990    1.0357

Concordance= 0.603  (se = 0.025 )
Likelihood ratio test= 14.12  on 2 df,   p=9e-04
Wald test            = 13.47  on 2 df,   p=0.001
Score (logrank) test = 13.72  on 2 df,   p=0.001

title: 3  Semi-Parametric Modelling
text:
3.4 Interpretation

3.4.1 Coefficients and hazard ratios
The raw coefficients \(\hat{\beta}\) are on the log-hazard-ratio scale. Exponentiating them gives hazard ratios directly. The {broom} package makes this tidy:

tidy(cox_fit, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)

# A tibble: 2 × 5
  term  estimate conf.low conf.high p.value
  <chr>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
1 sex      0.599    0.431     0.831 0.00218
2 age      1.02     0.999     1.04  0.0646 


Each hazard ratio represents the multiplicative change in the instantaneous hazard associated with a one-unit increase in the covariate, holding all other covariates constant.
For example, if sex has \(HR < 1\), female patients (coded 2) have a lower hazard of death relative to males, i.e. better survival after adjusting for age.


3.4.2 Confidence intervals
95% confidence intervals on the hazard ratio scale are obtained by exponentiating the Wald-based interval on the log scale: \(e^{\hat{\beta} \pm 1.96 \cdot SE(\hat{\beta})}\).


3.4.3 Global tests
summary() reports three global tests of whether any covariate has a significant effect:



Test
Basis




Likelihood ratio
Compares log-likelihoods of full vs null model


Wald
Based on \(\hat{\beta} / SE(\hat{\beta})\)


Score (log-rank)
Based on score function at \(\beta = 0\)



In large samples all three are equivalent, the likelihood ratio test is generally preferred.

title: 3  Semi-Parametric Modelling
text:
3.5 Estimating Baseline Hazard & Survival Function
Although the Cox model does not require specifying \(h_0(t)\), once we have estimated \(\hat{\beta}\)s we can recover a non-parametric estimate of the cumulative baseline hazard \(\hat{H}_0(t)\) and baseline Survival Function \(S_0(t)\) by setting all coefficient values to zero.






Centering Covariates



What is the interpretation of assuming the baseline survival or hazard rate is obtained by setting covariates to zero?
Does this make sense?
Should we considered centering our covariates to obtain more faithful estimates of baseline hazard curves?


By default basehaz() uses the mean of all covariates for computational stability:

Many textbooks refer to H(t; 0) as “the” baseline hazard for a Cox model; this is returned by the centered= FALSE option. However, due to potential overflow or underflow in the exp() function this can be a very bad idea in practice


# Cumulative baseline hazard (at mean of covariates by default)
bh <- basehaz(cox_fit, centered = T)  # centered=FALSE gives H0(t)
head(bh)

       hazard time
1 0.004188049    5
2 0.016872791   11
3 0.021155179   12
4 0.029801364   13
5 0.034164334   15
6 0.038553525   26


We can obtain baseline survival curve estimates using the result from Equation 3.1.

# Baseline survival S0(t) = exp(-H0(t))
bh$surv0 <- exp(-bh$hazard)
head(bh)

       hazard time     surv0
1 0.004188049    5 0.9958207
2 0.016872791   11 0.9832688
3 0.021155179   12 0.9790670
4 0.029801364   13 0.9706383
5 0.034164334   15 0.9664127
6 0.038553525   26 0.9621802

ggplot(bh, aes(time, surv0)) +
  geom_step() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1))








Comparing to the direct estimate from survfit2()

survfit2(cox_fit) |> 
  ggsurvfit::ggsurvfit()








More usefully, survfit() applied to a fitted Cox model produces survival curves at specified covariate values, resulting in a covariate-adjusted survival curve:

# Survival curve for a 60-year-old female (sex=2) 
new_patient <- data.frame(age = c(60, 60), sex = c(1, 2))
cox_surv <- survfit(cox_fit, newdata = new_patient)

plot(cox_surv, xlab = "Days", ylab = "S(t)", main = "Covariate-adjusted survival")

title: 3  Semi-Parametric Modelling
text:
3.6 Diagnostics
We need to check the basic statistical assumptions behind the Cox proportional hazards model.

Proportional hazards assumption

Survival time of one patient does not depend upon the survival time of another.

Uninformative Censoring


3.6.1 Proportional hazards assumption
The proportional hazards assumption states that the hazard ratio between any two covariate patterns is constant over time. Violation means the effect of a covariate changes as follow-up progresses.
The standard test uses scaled Schoenfeld residuals (cox.zph()). If the PH assumption holds, the residuals should show no trend over time, and the test \(p\)-value should not be small.

ph_test <- cox.zph(cox_fit)
ph_test

       chisq df    p
sex    2.608  1 0.11
age    0.209  1 0.65
GLOBAL 2.771  2 0.25



plot(ph_test)















A statistically significant result for a covariate (small \(p\)-value) suggests that covariate’s effect is not constant over time. Remedies include:

Adding a time-by-covariate interaction term
Stratifying on the offending variable (see Section below)
Fitting a time-varying coefficient model



3.6.2 Goodness of fit
Martingale residuals assess whether the functional form of each continuous covariate is appropriate. They lie in \((-\infty, 1]\); a LOESS smoother of residuals vs covariate values should be flat around zero if the linear form is correct.

lung_complete <- na.omit(lung[, c("time", "status", "age", "sex")])

mart_resid <- residuals(cox_fit, type = "martingale")

# Check functional form of age
ggplot(data.frame(age = lung_complete$age, resid = mart_resid), aes(age, resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Age", y = "Martingale residual")

`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









Deviance residuals (a normalised transform of martingale residuals) are more symmetric and useful for spotting poorly-fitted individuals:

dev_resid <- residuals(cox_fit, type = "deviance")

ggplot(data.frame(index = seq_along(dev_resid), resid = dev_resid), aes(index, resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-2, 2), linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  labs(x = "Observation index", y = "Deviance residual")








Points with \(|r_D| > 2\) are candidates for closer inspection.


3.6.3 Influence
dfbeta residuals estimate how much each coefficient changes if observation \(i\) is deleted. Large values flag influential observations.

dfbeta_resid <- residuals(cox_fit, type = "dfbeta")

# Plot influence on the 'age' coefficient (column 2)
ggplot(data.frame(index = seq_along(dfbeta_resid[, 2]), dfbeta = dfbeta_resid[, 2]),
       aes(index, dfbeta)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Observation index", y = "dfbeta (age coefficient)")

title: 3  Semi-Parametric Modelling
text:
3.7 Stratification
If a covariate violates the PH assumption but we still want to adjust for it, we can stratify on it. The model estimates a separate baseline hazard \(h_{0k}(t)\) for each stratum \(k\), while keeping the \(\beta\) coefficients common across strata.

cox_strat <- coxph(
  Surv(time, status) ~ age + strata(sex),
  data = lung
)

summary(cox_strat)

Call:
coxph(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ age + strata(sex), data = lung)

  n= 228, number of events= 165 

        coef exp(coef) se(coef)     z Pr(>|z|)  
age 0.016215  1.016347 0.009187 1.765   0.0776 .
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

    exp(coef) exp(-coef) lower .95 upper .95
age     1.016     0.9839    0.9982     1.035

Concordance= 0.546  (se = 0.026 )
Likelihood ratio test= 3.18  on 1 df,   p=0.07
Wald test            = 3.12  on 1 df,   p=0.08
Score (logrank) test = 3.12  on 1 df,   p=0.08








Note



Stratification removes the stratifying variable from the set of estimated hazard ratios. You cannot obtain a HR for sex from this model. Use stratification when you need to control for a variable but are not interested in its effect estimate.

title: 3  Semi-Parametric Modelling
text:
3.8 Time-dependent covariates
When a covariate’s value changes during follow-up (e.g., a drug dose, lab value, or treatment switch), the standard Cox model cannot handle it correctly. The solution is to expand the dataset into counting process format using (tstart, tstop] intervals.
It’s important that covariates only include information about the past and present. An example of where time dependent covariates can be used is when there is a change in medication because a new treatment becomes available. An example where it is not appropriate is when the medication is changed because the status of the patient deteriorates (is related to the outcome). This may then produce the counter-intuitive conclusion that changing the medication resulted in poorer survival.
We will use a short example from the Stanford Heart Transplant data.

# Illustrative example using the heart dataset 
head(heart)

  start stop event        age      year surgery transplant id
1     0   50     1 -17.155373 0.1232033       0          0  1
2     0    6     1   3.835729 0.2546201       0          0  2
3     0    1     0   6.297057 0.2655715       0          0  3
4     1   16     1   6.297057 0.2655715       0          1  3
5     0   36     0  -7.737166 0.4900753       0          0  4
6    36   39     1  -7.737166 0.4900753       0          1  4


The Surv(start, stop, event) three-argument form specifies the counting process:

cox_td <- coxph(
  Surv(start, stop, event) ~ transplant + age + year + surgery,
  data = heart
)

tidy(cox_td, exponentiate = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  select(term, estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value)

# A tibble: 4 × 5
  term        estimate conf.low conf.high p.value
  <chr>          <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>   <dbl>
1 transplant1    0.990    0.535     1.83   0.974 
2 age            1.03     1.00      1.06   0.0476
3 year           0.864    0.752     0.992  0.0378
4 surgery        0.529    0.257     1.09   0.0827








Caution



Time-dependent covariates must be defined using only past information — values known before the start of each interval. Using future information (e.g., a post-event measurement) introduces immortal time bias and will give misleading results.
Consider if we included a baseline covariate for obtaining a transplant at some point. Recieving (or not) a transplant leaks information about patient survival characteristics and will bias estimates of survival prior to the transplant occuring. Transplant patients had to “survive” the pre-transplant window to receive the organ, that waiting period is erroneously attributed as a survival benefit of the transplant itself.

title: 4  Parametric Modelling
text:
4.1 Why parametric models?
Parametric survival modelling makes assumptions about the statistical distribution of survival times. This makes it a more flexible approach, assuming you are able to find a suitable distribution to suit your data.
The Cox proportional hazards model is powerful because it leaves the baseline hazard \(h_0(t)\) unspecified. But this flexibility comes at a cost: the Cox model cannot directly answer questions that require a fully specified hazard function, such as:
The parametric approach also has higher efficiency, so may be preferable with small samples. There is also no need to comply with the proportional hazards assumption.
Parametric survival models address this by assuming that survival times follow a specific probability distribution. If the assumed distribution is a good approximation to reality, parametric models are more efficient (smaller standard errors) and enable richer predictions than the Cox model.

title: 4  Parametric Modelling
text:
What is the mean survival time?

What is the expected survival time for a new patient?
What is the probability of surviving beyond the limits of the empirical data?
How does the hazard function itself change over time?

title: 4  Parametric Modelling
text:
4.2 Common distributions
The key distributions used in parametric survival modelling all describe how the hazard function \(h(t)\) behaves over time.

4.2.1 Exponential
The simplest parametric model. The hazard is constant over time:
\[
h(t) = \lambda
\]
This implies no “ageing” — the probability of dying in the next instant is the same regardless of how long the subject has already survived. The survival function is:
\[
S(t) = e^{-\lambda t}
\]


4.2.2 Weibull
A generalisation of the exponential that allows for monotone (increasing or decreasing) hazards:
\[
h(t) = \lambda \gamma t^{\gamma - 1}
\]

\(\gamma > 1\): hazard increases over time (e.g. aging-related mortality)
\(\gamma = 1\): reduces to the exponential (constant hazard)
\(\gamma < 1\): hazard decreases over time (e.g. early post-operative risk)

The Weibull is the most commonly used parametric survival distribution.


4.2.3 Log-normal
Assumes \(\log(T) \sim \text{Normal}(\mu, \sigma^2)\). The hazard is non-monotone. It rises to a peak and then decreases. This is appropriate when mortality risk initially increases then declines (e.g. surgical recovery).


4.2.4 Summary








Distribution
Hazard shape
Typical use case




Exponential
Constant
Simple baselines, memoryless processes


Weibull
Monotone (inc. or dec.)
Most common; general-purpose


Log-normal
Unimodal (inc. then dec.)
Surgical recovery, infection clearance

title: 4  Parametric Modelling
text:
4.3 Parameterisation
Parametric survival models can be written in two equivalent (but differently interpreted) ways.

Accelerated failure time (AFT) model: Covariates act multiplicatively on time

Proportional hazards (PH) parameterisation: Covariates act multiplicatively on the hazard

The survreg() function in the survival package uses the AFT parameterisation.

4.3.1 Accelerated Failure Time (AFT) Models
Rather than assume a distribution for t_j the event times directly, lets assume a distributional form of:
\[
\tau_i = \exp{(-\textbf{x}_j\beta_x)}t_j
\]
So now we have an ‘acceleration’ factor of \(\exp{(-\textbf{x}_j\beta_x)}\)
If this value is > 1 then time will pass more quickly, so failure or death would occur sooner, and vice-versa.
Rearranging we get:
\[
t_j = \exp{(\textbf{x}_j\beta_x)} \tau_j
\] So we have a form where the coefficients have a multiplicative effect on event times.
We can write:
\[
\ln{(t_j)} = \textbf{x}_j\beta_x + \ln{(\tau_j)}
\]
Now we can describe event times \(T\) more generally in this way:
\[
T = \exp{(\beta_0 + \beta_1x)} \times \epsilon
\]
This allows a formulation where time must be positive. Also the error component \(\epsilon\) is conventionally accepted as exponentially distributed.
This can be linearized as:
\[
\log(T) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x + \epsilon^*
\]
Where \(\epsilon^* = \ln{\epsilon}\)
This results in the exponential version of the AFT model. If we allow a more general form, with a shape parameter, we can specify Weibull distributions.
\[
\log(T) = \beta_0 + \beta_1x + \sigma \times\epsilon^*
\]

title: 4  Parametric Modelling
text:
4.4 Fitting parametric models with survreg()
survreg() fits AFT models for a range of distributions. The syntax is similar to coxph(), but you specify a dist argument.

# Weibull AFT model on the lung dataset
fit_weibull <- survreg(
  Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex,
  data = lung,
  dist = "weibull"
)

summary(fit_weibull)


Call:
survreg(formula = Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex, data = lung, 
    dist = "weibull")
               Value Std. Error     z       p
(Intercept)  6.27485    0.48137 13.04 < 2e-16
age         -0.01226    0.00696 -1.76  0.0781
sex          0.38209    0.12748  3.00  0.0027
Log(scale)  -0.28230    0.06188 -4.56 5.1e-06

Scale= 0.754 

Weibull distribution
Loglik(model)= -1147.1   Loglik(intercept only)= -1153.9
    Chisq= 13.59 on 2 degrees of freedom, p= 0.0011 
Number of Newton-Raphson Iterations: 5 
n= 228 


The (Intercept) is \(\mu\) (the log-time intercept) and Log(scale) is \(\log(\sigma)\), which is related to the Weibull shape parameter \(\gamma = 1/\sigma\).

4.4.1 Comparing distributions
It is good practice to compare several distributions using AIC or BIC. We fit the same model under four distributions and compare:

dists <- c("weibull", "exponential", "lognormal")

fits <- map(dists, \(d) survreg(
  Surv(time, status) ~ age + sex,
  data = lung,
  dist = d
))

tibble(
  distribution = dists,
  loglik       = map_dbl(fits, logLik),
  n_params     = map_dbl(fits, \(f) length(coef(f)) + 1),
  AIC          = map_dbl(fits, AIC),
  BIC          = map_dbl(fits, BIC)
) |>
  arrange(AIC)

# A tibble: 3 × 5
  distribution loglik n_params   AIC   BIC
  <chr>         <dbl>    <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
1 weibull      -1147.        4 2302. 2316.
2 exponential  -1156.        4 2318. 2328.
3 lognormal    -1159.        4 2326. 2339.


Lower AIC indicates a better balance of fit and parsimony. The exponential model is nested within the Weibull (\(\sigma = 1\), i.e. \(\gamma = 1\)), so a formal likelihood ratio test is also possible.

title: 4  Parametric Modelling
text:
4.5 Interpreting coefficients
survreg() returns coefficients on the log-time scale (AFT). Exponentiating gives the time ratio — the multiplicative change in expected survival time per unit increase in the covariate.
A coefficient \(\beta_j > 0\) means covariate \(x_j\) increases survival time — patients live longer. The time ratio \(e^{\beta_j}\) gives the multiplicative factor by which expected survival time changes per unit increase in \(x_j\).

tidy(fit_weibull, conf.int = TRUE) |>
  filter(term != "Log(scale)") |>
  mutate(
    time_ratio   = exp(estimate),
    tr_conf.low  = exp(conf.low),
    tr_conf.high = exp(conf.high)
  ) |>
  select(term, estimate, time_ratio, tr_conf.low, tr_conf.high, p.value)

# A tibble: 3 × 6
  term        estimate time_ratio tr_conf.low tr_conf.high  p.value
  <chr>          <dbl>      <dbl>       <dbl>        <dbl>    <dbl>
1 (Intercept)   6.27      531.        207.         1364.   7.69e-39
2 age          -0.0123      0.988       0.974         1.00 7.81e- 2
3 sex           0.382       1.47        1.14          1.88 2.72e- 3








AFT vs HR interpretation



A time ratio of 0.8 for a covariate means that subjects with one extra unit of that covariate have survival times that are, on average, 20% shorter. A hazard ratio > 1 means increased hazard (worse survival); a time ratio < 1 also means shorter survival. Both encode the same relationship, but on different scales.

title: 4  Parametric Modelling
text:
4.6 Survival curves from parametric models
Because the full distribution is specified, we can predict smooth survival curves at any covariate pattern.

new_patients <- expand_grid(
  time = seq(1, 900, by = 5),
  age = c(60, 60),
  sex = c(1, 2) # 1 = male, 2 = female
)

new_patients |>
  mutate(
    lp = predict(fit_weibull, newdata = new_patients, type = "lp"),
    surv = 1 - pweibull(time, shape = 1 / fit_weibull$scale, scale = exp(lp))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(time, surv, colour = factor(sex))) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    x = "Days",
    y = "S(t)",
    colour = "Sex",
    title = "Parametric Weibull survival curves",
    subtitle = "Age 60"
  )

title: 5  Workflow
text:
5.1 Exploratory Analysis
A standard workflow for approaching survival analysis is given below. This will change for any given analysis, but forms a useful starting point.

title: 5  Workflow
text:
Check number of failures is sufficient: For each level of categorical variables to be included in the model there should usually be a minimum of about 10. If there are not sufficient for one level of a category, it may be possible to rectify this by merging categories, but only with the guidance of a subject matter expert.
Plot the distribution of continuous predictors: This is typically achieved through histograms or other univariate methods. Highly skewed distributions may be good candidates for transformations. It is also useful to check for associations between variables using cross tabulation, scatterplots etc.

title: 5  Workflow
text:
5.2 Kaplan-Meier Plots
As an exploratory technique, Kaplan-Meier plots can be made for the entire marginal survival data, however there is significant benefit in stratifying these plots by the categorical variables in your data. Furthermore, continuous variables can be discretized into 2 or 3 levels and the Kaplan-Meier curves compared.

title: 5  Workflow
text:
5.3 Model Building
Some authors suggest a step-wise process for model fitting. These methods should be used with caution and a deeper appreication for the scientific merics of including/excluding variables, and not as a dogmatic exercise. The following guide is adapted from Hosmer Jr, Lemeshow, and May (2008):

Conduct univariate analysis to detect significant differences in survival curves for each variable.
Fit a multivariable model containing all variables significant in the univariable analysis at the 20-25 percent level.
Use the p-values from the Wald tests of the individual coefficients to identify covariates that might be deleted from the model.
Following the fit of the reduced model, we assess whether removal of the covariate has produced an ‘important’ change in the coefficients of the variables remaining in the model. If the variable excluded is an important confounder, it should be added back into the model. This process continues until no covariates can be deleted from the model.
At this point, we add to the model, one at a time, all variables excluded from the initial multivariable model to confirm that they are neither statistically significant nor an important confounder.
Test for the addition of more complex interaction terms.

title: 5  Workflow
text:
5.4 Diagnostics

Check proportional hazards and modify model if required. A useful measures to control for violation of the proportional hazards assumption is to stratify by the offending variable.
Check diagnostics for final model:

Proportional hazards
Cox-Snell

dfBeta
